options.why: Divided by $n(L) = 9$ instead of $n(C) = 18$, which reverses the condition and gives $P(C \mid L)$.
Kept the whole survey of $28$ as the denominator, so this is $P(L \cap C)$ and ignores the reduced sample space.
Gave the unconditional $P(L)$ by using the whole $L$ circle over the whole survey.

questions.solution_text:
The condition is $C$, so the sample space is reduced to the $5 + 13 = 18$ students in $C$.
Of those $18$, the $5$ in the overlap are left-handed.
$P(L \mid C) = \frac{n(L \cap C)}{n(C)}$
$= \frac{5}{18}$

questions.question_text:
The two-way table shows the lunch orders placed by $72$ students at a school canteen.
$\begin{array}{l|c|c|c} & \text{Year 7} & \text{Year 8} & \text{Total} \\ \hline \text{Hot food} & 24 & 12 & 36 \\ \text{Sandwich} & 16 & 20 & 36 \\ \hline \text{Total} & 40 & 32 & 72 \end{array}$
One order is chosen at random. Find the probability that it is hot food, given that it was placed by a Year $8$ student, as a fraction in simplest form.

options.why: Divided the $12$ by the hot food row total of $36$, which reverses the condition and gives $P(\text{Year } 8 \mid \text{hot food})$.
Used the grand total of $72$ as the denominator instead of the Year $8$ column total.
Gave the unconditional probability of a Year $8$ order by using $32$ out of $72$.

questions.solution_text:
The condition restricts the sample space to the Year $8$ column, whose total is $32$.
Of those $32$ orders, $12$ are hot food.
$P(\text{hot food} \mid \text{Year } 8) = \frac{12}{32}$
$= \frac{3}{8}$

questions.question_text: In a class of $32$ students, $20$ walk to school, $14$ have a part-time job and $9$ both walk and have a part-time job. One student is chosen at random. Find the probability that the student walks to school, given that they have a part-time job, as a fraction in simplest form.

options.why: Conditioned on walking instead of on having a job, so this is $P(\text{job} \mid \text{walks})$.
Used the whole class of $32$ as the denominator instead of reducing the sample space to the job holders.
Gave the unconditional probability of having a part-time job, $14$ out of $32$, ignoring the condition.

questions.solution_text:
The condition is 'has a part-time job', so the sample space is reduced to those $14$ students.
Of those $14$, the $9$ who also walk are favourable.
$P(\text{walks} \mid \text{job}) = \frac{9}{14}$

questions.question_text: Let $B$ be the event 'a student catches the bus to school' and $J$ be the event 'a student has a part-time job'. Which expression represents 'the probability that a student catches the bus, knowing that they have a part-time job'?

options.why: Writes the events in the order the words appear, putting the event before the bar and the condition first.
Reads 'knowing that' as 'and', so no reduction of the sample space is made.
Ignores the condition altogether and gives the unconditional probability of catching the bus.

questions.solution_text:
'Knowing that they have a part-time job' names the condition, so $J$ goes after the bar.
The event asked about is catching the bus, so $B$ goes before the bar.
$P(B \mid J)$

options.text: They divided by $n(J) = 15$ instead of $n(B) = 24$, so they have found $P(B \mid J)$ instead.
They divided by the whole sample space of $36$ instead of reducing it to the condition.
options.why: Confuses the reduced-sample-space error with the reversal error; using $36$ would have produced $\frac{8}{36}$, not $\frac{8}{15}$.

options.text: They used $n(J \cap B)$ as the numerator when $n(B)$ was needed.
options.why: Believes the condition supplies the numerator, when the condition supplies the denominator and the overlap supplies the numerator.

options.text: They included the $5$ students in neither event in the reduced sample space.
options.why: Assumes the outside region joins the condition, when the condition removes every student outside $B$.

questions.solution_text:
The condition is $B$, so the denominator must be $n(B) = 8 + 16 = 24$.
The student used $n(J) = 7 + 8 = 15$, which is the denominator for the reversed conditional.
$\frac{8}{15} = P(B \mid J)$
$P(J \mid B) = \frac{8}{24}$
$= \frac{1}{3}$

options.text: It reduces the sample space from $45$ students to the $27$ students in $B$.
It reduces the sample space from $45$ students to the $9$ students in both events.
options.why: Confuses the reduced sample space with the reduced event space, which is the overlap $J \cap B$.

options.text: It reduces the sample space from $45$ students to the $15$ students in $J$.
options.why: Reduces to the event being asked about rather than to the event named by the condition.

options.text: It leaves the sample space at $45$ students and changes only the favourable outcomes.
options.why: Treats a condition as narrowing the numerator only, so the denominator is never reduced.

questions.solution_text:
The condition rules out every student outside $B$, so the $6$ in $J$ only and the $12$ in neither event are removed.
$n(B) = 9 + 18$
$= 27$
The sample space is reduced from $45$ students to those $27$ bus catchers, and the denominator becomes $27$.

questions.question_text: At a large school, $P(B) = 0.4$, $P(J) = 0.25$ and $P(J \cap B) = 0.14$, where $B$ is 'a student catches the bus to school' and $J$ is 'a student has a part-time job'. Find $P(J \mid B)$ as a decimal.

options.why: Divided by $P(J)$ instead of $P(B)$, which reverses the condition and gives $P(B \mid J)$.
Stopped at the intersection probability without dividing by the probability of the condition.
Gave the unconditional $P(J)$, ignoring the reduction of the sample space to $B$.

questions.solution_text:
The condition is $B$, so the denominator is $P(B)$.
$P(J \mid B) = \frac{P(J \cap B)}{P(B)}$
$= \frac{0.14}{0.4}$
$= 0.35$

questions.question_text: At a large school, $30\%$ of students are left-handed and $60\%$ catch the bus to school. Being left-handed and catching the bus are independent events. Find $P(L \mid B)$ as a percentage, where $L$ is 'the student is left-handed' and $B$ is 'the student catches the bus'.

options.why: Swapped the event and the condition, giving $P(B \mid L)$ rather than $P(L \mid B)$.
Divided $30\%$ by $60\%$ as though $P(L)$ were the intersection probability.
Multiplied $30\%$ by $60\%$, which gives $P(L \cap B)$ rather than the conditional probability.

questions.solution_text:
The events are independent, so knowing that a student catches the bus gives no new information about being left-handed.
The bus catchers contain the same proportion of left-handed students as the whole school.
$P(L \mid B) = P(L)$
$= 30\%$

questions.question_text: In a survey of $48$ students, $30$ catch the bus to school, $22$ have a part-time job and $8$ do neither. One student is chosen at random. Find the probability that the student has a part-time job, given that they catch the bus, as a fraction in simplest form.

options.why: Divided the $12$ in both events by the $22$ job holders, which reverses the condition and gives $P(B \mid J)$.
Used the whole survey of $48$ as the denominator instead of reducing it to the bus catchers.
Gave the unconditional probability of having a part-time job, $22$ out of $48$.
